'''George Chappell Schatz''' (born April 14, 1949), the Morrison Professor of Chemistry at [[Northwestern University]],  is a [[theoretical chemistry|theoretical chemist]] best known for his seminal contributions to the fields of [[reaction dynamics]] and [[nanotechnology]].

==Early life and career==
Born in [[Watertown, New York]] and raised in [[Sackets Harbor, New York]], he obtained his B. S. in [[chemistry]] from [[Clarkson University]] in 1971.<ref name="acs_pub_profile">{{cite web |title=Editor Profile |url=https://pubs.acs.org/page/jpclcd/profile.html |website=ACS Publications |publisher=[[American Chemical Society]] |accessdate=20 August 2018 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20180820155629/https://pubs.acs.org/page/jpclcd/profile.html |archivedate=20 August 2018 |language=en}}</ref> At Clarkson, he was mentored by organic chemistry professor Richard Partsch, who encouraged him to spend a summer working at [[Argonne National Laboratory]] in 1971. He went on to earn a Ph.D. from [[California Institute of Technology|Caltech]] in 1976<ref name="acs_pub_profile" /> under [[Aron Kuppermann]]. While working on his doctorate, he took classes taught by [[Richard Feynman]] on [[quantum electrodynamics]] and [[particle physics]]. Following postdoctoral work at [[MIT]] under [[John Ross (chemist)|John Ross]], he joined the chemistry department at [[Northwestern University]]. Schatz is a member of the [[Center for Chemistry at the Space-Time Limit]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Mossman |first=Kaspar |date=2007-12-26 |title=Profile of George Schatz |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |language=en |volume=104 |issue=52 |pages=20654–20655 |doi=10.1073/pnas.0710466104 |doi-access=free |issn=0027-8424 |pmc=2409209 |pmid=18093942|bibcode=2007PNAS..10420654M }}</ref>

To date he has co-authored over 1000 scientific papers<ref>{{Cite web |date=August 3, 2023 |title=Professor George C. Schatz |url=https://sites.northwestern.edu/schatz/people/george-schatz/ |website=The Schatz Group}}</ref> and co-authored two books with his colleague [[Mark A. Ratner]]: ''Introduction to Quantum Mechanics in Chemistry'' and ''Quantum Mechanics in Chemistry.'' Recently much of Schatz's research has been concerned with [[nanotechnology]] and [[bionanotechnology]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mielke |first1=Steven L. |last2=Belytschko |first2=Ted |last3=Schatz |first3=George C. |date=May 5, 2007 |title=Nanoscale Fraction Mechanics |journal=[[Annual Review of Physical Chemistry]] |volume=58 |pages=185–209|doi=10.1146/annurev.physchem.58.032806.104502 |pmid=17059367 |bibcode=2007ARPC...58..185M }}</ref> His work has collectively received over 130,000 citations,<ref>{{Cite web |date=August 3, 2023 |title=Google Scholar: George C. Schatz |url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=XHtII_oAAAAJ&hl=en}}</ref> including a 2003 article on the optical properties of nanoparticles which has been cited more than 12,000 times.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kelly |first1=K. Lance |last2=Coronado |first2=Eduardo |last3=Zhao |first3=Lin Lin |last4=Schatz |first4=George C. |date=2003-01-01 |title=The Optical Properties of Metal Nanoparticles: The Influence of Size, Shape, and Dielectric Environment |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/jp026731y |journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry B |language=en |volume=107 |issue=3 |pages=668–677 |doi=10.1021/jp026731y |issn=1520-6106|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

A longtime senior editor of the ''[[Journal of Physical Chemistry]]'', he became its editor-in-chief in 2005. The journal previously (1997) having been split in ''[[Journal of Physical Chemistry A]]'' (molecular physical chemistry, both theoretical and experimental) and ''[[Journal of Physical Chemistry B]]'' (solid state, soft matter, liquids), Schatz initiated the spin-off of a third journal, ''[[Journal of Physical Chemistry C]]'', focusing on [[nanotechnology]] and [[molecular electronics]].

==Awards and honors==
Schatz is a [[Fellow of the American Physical Society]] (1987) and a member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] (2007) and the [[International Academy of Quantum Molecular Science]].  Schatz has won the Ahmed Zewail Prize award of the journal [[Chemical Physics Letters]] for "outstanding contributions to the theory and understanding of gas-phase reaction dynamics, plasmonics, and nanostructured materials". The biennial prize was developed by Elsevier to honor Nobel laureate [[Ahmed Zewail]], who was a longtime editor of the journal.
